brief.story:
On Friday, September 18, 2026, U.S. Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5), Co-Chair of the House AI Commission and a senior member of the House Intelligence Committee, announced a new bipartisan agenda to put guardrails on AI development. He made the announcement at an event at Fairleigh Dickinson University in Teaneck.

The American AI Security Act

Gottheimer announced the American AI Security Act, legislation co-led with Rep. Mike Lawler (R-NY), that would create a mandatory government review process for advanced AI models ahead of their release. The reviews would be led by the National Security Agency and would last for 30 days, with the possibility of a single 30-day extension.

The National Security Agency would have full access to determine if the model could be used to launch a cyberattack or help build chemical, biological, or radiological weapons. Per the official press release, companies would be able to provide technical support for the reviews, and appeal decisions through an expedited process modeled on the courts already used for national security cases.

Gottheimer framed the bill as filling a concrete policy gap: "Right now, there are no mandatory requirements for pre-deployment testing of frontier AI models," he said. "That doesn't work in banking, it doesn't work in food safety, it doesn't work in medicine, and it sure as hell shouldn't work with the technology that experts say could help build a bioweapon or take down our power grid. This isn't about stopping AI or stifling innovation, it is about making sure — with warning signs flashing red — that we can safely deploy AI, and win the race the right way."

Gottheimer's plan broadly follows the Trump administration's existing vetting regime for advanced AI models, which came together in chaotic fashion this summer in response to cybersecurity risks raised by new models from OpenAI and Anthropic. The White House has kept specifics of that process under wraps. The official press release states the current administration process is voluntary, based on a June 2026 Executive Order, and Gottheimer's bill would codify mandatory pre-deployment review in law.

Lawler co-sponsor quote, from the official press release: "Artificial intelligence is one of the most consequential technologies of our time, and we have a responsibility to make sure it strengthens our national security rather than becoming a tool for those who seek to harm Americans. The American AI Security Act takes a commonsense approach: before the most powerful AI models are deployed, we should know whether they could be used to launch devastating cyberattacks or facilitate the development of chemical, biological, or radiological weapons."

The China FIREWALL Act

The China FIREWALL Act, co-led by Republican Rep. Nick LaLota of New York, would prohibit Chinese-developed open-weight AI models from government-issued devices and bar federal agencies from purchasing software that relies on those models. According to Gottheimer's office, the proposal would expand on restrictions involving the Chinese AI model DeepSeek included in the fiscal 2026 National Defense Authorization Act by covering other Chinese-developed open-weight models used by federal agencies.

In his prepared remarks (official press release), Gottheimer named specific models still in use: "other Chinese open-weight models, like Moonshot's Kimi K3 and Alibaba's Qwen, are still walking right through the front door of our federal agencies, and they can still buy software with these models baked in without anyone even knowing it."

The letter to the National Cyber Director

Gottheimer also said he is sending a letter to Sean Cairncross, the President's Cyber Director, seeking information about the administration's AI cybersecurity clearinghouse and its ability to address threats involving autonomous AI-driven cyberattacks. In his remarks, Gottheimer questioned whether the clearinghouse is "built for the threat we're facing in 2026, or the threat we were facing two years ago," and raised whether the AI supply chain itself should be treated as critical infrastructure.

Legislative outlook

There is growing public pressure for federal legislators to take action on AI regulation and a growing sense among lawmakers that bipartisan legislation is necessary. However, Gottheimer acknowledged in his remarks that Republican leadership has refused to bring AI safety legislation to the floor for a vote, and called on the Speaker to reconvene Congress before the election to pass the bills. The sources do not say when or whether a vote is scheduled.

sourceTexts.text:
Above: Gottheimer announces new AI safety legislation at FDU.

TEANECK, NJ — Today, Friday, September 18, 2026, U.S. Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5), Co-Chair of the House AI Commission and a senior member of the House Intelligence Committee, announced a new bipartisan agenda to put real guardrails on AI development to ensure the U.S. can win the global AI race in the right way.

Watch Gottheimer’s remarks here.

“Right now, there are no mandatory requirements for pre-deployment testing of frontier AI models,” said Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5). “That doesn’t work in banking, it doesn’t work in food safety, it doesn’t work in medicine, and it sure as hell shouldn’t work with the technology that experts say could help build a bioweapon or take down our power grid. This isn’t about stopping AI or stifling innovation, it is about making sure — with warning signs flashing red — that we can safely deploy AI, and win the race the right way.

“Artificial intelligence is one of the most consequential technologies of our time, and we have a responsibility to make sure it strengthens our national security rather than becoming a tool for those who seek to harm Americans. The American AI Security Act takes a commonsense approach: before the most powerful AI models are deployed, we should know whether they could be used to launch devastating cyberattacks or facilitate the development of chemical, biological, or radiological weapons,” said Congressman Mike Lawler (NY-17).

Gottheimer’s AI safety agenda includes two new bipartisan pieces of federal legislation  and an inquiry into the Administration’s new cybersecurity plan, including:

The American AI Security Act, co-led by Congressman Mike Lawler (NY-17), establishes a mandatory, pre-deployment national security review for the most powerful AI models. Before releasing a covered model, developers would be required to give the National Security Agency full access to evaluate whether it could be used to launch a serious cyberattack or help build a chemical, biological, or radiological weapon. The review operates on a firm clock — 30 days, with a single 30-day extension if needed — so it functions as a serious national security check rather than either a rubber stamp or endless bureaucracy. Companies would be able to provide technical support for the reviews, and appeal decisions through an expedited process modeled on the courts already used for national security cases.

The China FIREWALL Act, co-led by Congressman Nick LaLota (NY-1), keeps Chinese-developed AI off of U.S. government systems. The bill would ban all Chinese-developed open-weight AI models from government-issued devices and prohibit federal agencies from procuring software that relies on those models. The legislation builds on Gottheimer’s No DeepSeek on Government Devices Act, which became law as part of the FY26 National Defense Authorization Act and blocked the Chinese AI model DeepSeek from federal devices. The China FIREWALL Act closes the loophole that still allows other Chinese open-weight models to be used at federal agencies.

And finally, Gottheimer announced he is sending a letter to Sean Cairncross, the President’s Cyber Director, about the Administration’s new AI cybersecurity clearinghouse and how it can help the government respond to growing fears of autonomous cyberattacks.

The announcement was made at Fairleigh Dickinson University, which is launching a new state-of-the-art Health Humanics Innovation Hub, that’s designed to train the next generation of healthcare workers to use AI tools without losing the human being in front of them.

Gottheimer was joined by New Jersey State Senator Gordon Johnson, Teaneck Mayor Mark Schwartz, FDU Senior VP of Government Affairs, Robert Pignatello, Engineer Lab Director, Reggie Joseph, and students from Fairleigh Dickinson University.

Below: Gottheimer announces new AI safety legislation at FDU.

Gottheimer’s remarks as prepared for delivery.Thank you all for having me here today, and thank you to Fairleigh Dickinson University for opening up your campus for a discussion on this critical topic.

Now, I’ve been to a lot of events at a lot of great institutions across the Fifth District, but I want to take a second to recognize FDU, because this school has a story worth telling.

It started in 1942, right down the road in Rutherford, as a little two-year junior college founded by Peter and Sally Sammartino. Today, it’s the largest private university in the entire state of New Jersey, with 12,000 students, more than 100 degree programs, and students coming here from all over the world.  It’s a great American story of true leadership.

Speaking of leadership, President Avaltroni and his team have built something they call “Humanics.” The idea is simple: as AI gets built into everything, especially health care, you don’t throw out empathy, ethics, and equity.

You build them in from day one. They’re standing up a Health Humanics Innovation Hub right here on the Metropolitan Campus, which Senator Johnson helped secure funding for, that brings together a healthcare humanity lab, a storytelling data lab, and partnerships with Epic Systems to make sure the doctors and nurses of tomorrow know how to use these tools without losing sight of the human being in front of them. That’s exactly the mindset we need to bring to the AI policy debate right now – as the AI race accelerates, we have to remember that the benefits of innovation are boundless in the new opportunities they offer, but can be equally boundless in the new threats they pose.

AI can change the world. It can make our businesses more productive, help Americans develop new skills, strengthen our national security, and keep the United States at the forefront of technological innovation, especially in the competition with China. It can make incredible discoveries in medicine; it can personalize education, make government more efficient and accessible, and help workers focus more on key decisions.

But, as we learned in the last weeks with Hugging Face, and yesterday, with more disclosures from OpenAI of rogue agents with basically a mind of their own, the downsides of this transformative technology, if not controlled, are real.

In these cases, agents deceived their developers, coordinated amongst themselves, and escaped from what were supposed to be secure sandboxes. If this technology gets into the wrong hands, you can imagine the potential for destruction – cybersecurity, biosecurity, our national security.  Used maliciously, the government of China or Iran or a non-state actor could wreak havoc on the world.  Two weeks ago, an engineer from Anthropic quit his job, declaring that this technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade.” As Bill Gates recently put it, “AI models could begin to act against our interests, and we could lose control.”

As I just mentioned, last month, a swarm of AI agents broke out of a locked-down sandbox test, found a security hole nobody even knew existed, and used it to hack straight into Hugging Face — one of the biggest and most important AI platforms on the planet. Hundreds of AI agents were coordinating with each other on a hidden message board, running for days all on their own, and they even lied to their programmers about what they did. That incident was one of the most alarming AI-driven cybersecurity failures on record — and it was conducted without any human oversight. That might sound like a movie plot or an unreleased Terminator sequel, but unfortunately it’s not.

And that’s not the only warning sign. Two weeks ago, a researcher who worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic made headlines when he quit his job at Anthropic and posted publicly that the industry is racing toward superintelligence and, in his words, gambling with our lives. That single post got 150 million views in just a day and a half. That should tell you something about how many Americans are scared of AI’s risks, and how few of them think anyone in Washington has their back. And in response, several of the leading AI CEOs acknowledged the technology’s dangers.

The runaway agents are just one of many new challenges AI poses — there are issues related to energy, water, and data centers; deepfakes, disinformation, and discrimination; chip policy and the need to protect our children; effects on the workforce. The list goes on.

And, when you’re in a race like this one, there is a great deal of pressure to go faster, both between our leading frontier labs — including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta — and between nations, particularly our competition with the Chinese Communist Party.

Ultimately, like in the Cold War, it will decide who has the military and economic might, which countries ally with others, and who will lead the world in areas like science, health care, and the humanities. While I believe deeply that we can’t afford to lose this race, we must win in the right way, or we like during the nuclear arms race, ultimately, we will all lose. I don’t mean to sound dark, but, as a member of the Intelligence Committee and Co-Chair of the House AI Commission, I have seen the briefings.

This is not a hypothetical threat. I’ve concluded that we are at a critical crossroads … on the precipice of changes that none of us can even imagine … and either we are going to get it right, or the ramifications will be unimaginable.   This is happening now, and Congress needs to act like it.

This morning, I want to focus on one area of that race that is central to how we protect our children, our families, and our national security — and that is how we test the latest AI frontier models before they are let out into the wild … before the public is able to utilize them.

Right now, there are no mandatory requirements for pre-deployment testing. We are solely reliant on the Trump Administration’s voluntary cybersecurity review process based on a June 2026 Executive Order. It’s caused mass confusion in the AI world – nobody really knows who’s covered, what the rules actually are, or what happens if you don’t play along. It seems nuts to me that we wouldn’t want to require testing from the best and brightest in our government before these models are released — to protect our cybersecurity, biosecurity, critical infrastructure — our families and our national security.

But, that’s where we are here. And why? Because there are many who believe that the AI labs can handle it themselves – or, as some of the founders suggested this past week, that they rely on third-party testers or auditors to handle it. My problem with that is multi-fold: one, there are very few of these outside testers; they have limited people, compute, and access to the labs; they lack national security clearances; they don’t have broad enough expertise on the threats posed, and they rely, in part, on the labs themselves for funding.  In short, it’s like having the fox guard the hen house.

It doesn’t work in banking, it doesn’t work in food safety, it doesn’t work in medicine, and it sure as hell shouldn’t work with technology that experts say could help build a bioweapon or take down our power grid. The answer isn’t, like some have suggested, to just shut it all down. That’s not tenable. Like it or not, AI is here.  We can’t just cede the race to China.  If we panic or stop AI development, we won’t actually stop AI — that’s not a safeguard. China is not slowing down for anybody. We will just hand the future to Beijing. It will put us right in the bullseye of our adversary.  We will just get someone else’s AI.

That brings me to what we’re actually doing about it.

First, I’m announcing the American AI Security Act — new bipartisan federal legislation that I’m introducing with Congressman Mike Lawler of New York. This bill ensures that before any company releases one of the most powerful AI models in the world, they have to give the government full access to evaluate it first — to check whether that model could be used to launch a serious cyberattack, attack our critical infrastructure, or help build a chemical, biological, or radiological weapon.

It’s a real, time-bounded review that other frontier developers can help coordinate. Not endless bureaucracy, but also not a rubber stamp. A serious national security check, with a deadline, with industry input, and a proper appeals process modeled on the courts we already use for national security cases. This isn’t about stopping AI or stifling innovation; it is about making sure — with warning signs flashing red — that we can safely deploy AI, and win the race the right way.

Second, I’m announcing the China FIREWALL Act to stop Chinese AI on all government systems.

Right now, DeepSeek is blocked on most federal devices — because I fought to put that block in place, through my No DeepSeek on Government Devices Act. It became law through last year’s defense spending bill. But, here’s the problem: other Chinese open-weight models, like Moonshot’s Kimi K3 and Alibaba’s Qwen, are still walking right through the front door of our federal agencies, and they can still buy software with these models baked in without anyone even knowing it.

So, alongside Congressman Nick LaLota of New York, I’m introducing this new bipartisan legislation to close that loophole for good — banning Chinese-developed open-weight models from government devices, and blocking agencies from procuring software that relies on them. If we can’t trust Beijing with our data, we shouldn’t allow our government to use their AI systems.

Third, I’m sending a letter to the President’s Cyber Director about the Administration’s new AI cybersecurity clearinghouse. Look, the idea behind it is the right one. But right now, it’s only built to catch known vulnerabilities. That is, the stuff we already know to look for.

It does nothing about what happens when you’ve got swarms of AI agents operating at machine speed, coordinating attacks faster than any human can respond. My letter asks the hard question: is this clearinghouse actually built for the threat we’re facing in 2026, or the threat we were facing two years ago? And it raises whether the AI supply chain itself should be treated as critical infrastructure, the same way we treat our power grid and our water systems. If AI breaks, everything built on top of it breaks with it.

This Congress alone, I’ve led more than a dozen bipartisan bills that put up immediate guardrails to keep pace with the rapid rise of AI.

There is nothing partisan about protecting our country. That’s why I’ve repeatedly teamed up with Republican and Democratic colleagues alike – and why I’m co-chairing the new AI Problem Solvers Task Force. My bills tackle critical issues from rogue AI agents and cybersecurity to commonsense consumer and child protections to AI digital literacy. These bills would both protect our families and national security, and ensure we can seize upon the opportunities ahead of us.

Unfortunately, Republican leadership has refused to directly bring any of these critical pieces of legislation to the floor for a vote. And they sent us home from Washington without acting. I think that’s a huge mistake — and, right now, every week matters for America’s safety. I strongly urge the Speaker to bring us back before the election to pass AI safety legislation like the bills I’m proposing today.

Finally, let me ask this question: How did another generation handle a technology terrifying enough to end the world, without either burying their heads in the sand or torching the relationship with their biggest rival? Go back to the Cold War.

The United States and the Soviet Union were racing each other on nuclear weapons — real enemies, real stakes, real distrust. And yet, at the height of that rivalry, President Kennedy stood up and said something that still holds up today. He said, “Among the traits the peoples of our two countries have in common, none is stronger than our mutual abhorrence of war.” Soon after, we signed a nuclear test ban treaty with the Soviets. We never stopped competing with them, but we understood that some risks are big enough that even fierce rivals have to keep the guardrails up.

That is exactly the balance we need with AI: compete like hell to win, and put real safety rails in place so winning doesn’t destroy us in the process.

Our country has never been a country that waits around scared of the future — we go out, and we build it, safely, and better than anyone else on Earth. The choice is not between innovation and responsibility. We need both. We need Americans to know that as AI becomes more powerful, there are commonsense guardrails in place.

I believe that if we keep working together across the aisle for our future, in the greatest country in the world, our best days will always be ahead of us.

Thank you, God bless you, and God bless the United States of America.

###

sourceTexts.title: Gottheimer announces bipartisan bills aimed at AI security, Chinese-developed models
sourceTexts.text:
(Photo: Gottheimer announces new AI safety legislation at FDU. Courtesy photo for WRNJ)

TEANECK, N.J. (Bergen County) — U.S. Rep. Josh Gottheimer on Friday announced two bipartisan bills focused on artificial intelligence security, including proposed federal reviews of powerful AI models before their release and restrictions on Chinese-developed AI models used by the federal government.

Gottheimer, D-N.J., announced the American AI Security Act and China FIREWALL Act during an event at Fairleigh Dickinson University in Teaneck. He also announced plans to seek information from National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross about the administration’s AI cybersecurity efforts.

“Right now, there are no mandatory requirements for pre-deployment testing of frontier AI models,” said Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5). “That doesn’t work in banking, it doesn’t work in food safety, it doesn’t work in medicine, and it sure as hell shouldn’t work with the technology that experts say could help build a bioweapon or take down our power grid. This isn’t about stopping AI or stifling innovation, it is about making sure — with warning signs flashing red — that we can safely deploy AI, and win the race the right way.”

The American AI Security Act, co-led by Republican Rep. Mike Lawler of New York, would establish a mandatory national security review for certain advanced AI models before they are released. Under the proposal, developers of covered models would be required to provide the National Security Agency access to evaluate whether the technology could be used to conduct a serious cyberattack or assist in developing chemical, biological or radiological weapons.

The proposed review would have a 30-day deadline, with one additional 30-day extension permitted if needed. Companies could provide technical assistance during the review and appeal decisions through an expedited process.

The China FIREWALL Act, co-led by Republican Rep. Nick LaLota of New York, would prohibit Chinese-developed open-weight AI models from government-issued devices and bar federal agencies from purchasing software that relies on those models.

According to Gottheimer’s office, the proposal would expand on restrictions involving the Chinese AI model DeepSeek included in the fiscal 2026 National Defense Authorization Act by covering other Chinese-developed open-weight models used by federal agencies.

Gottheimer also said he is sending a letter to Cairncross seeking information about the administration’s AI cybersecurity clearinghouse and its ability to address threats involving autonomous AI-driven cyberattacks. Cairncross recently said the administration is seeking to balance AI innovation with securing U.S. systems and preventing the technology from being misused by adversaries.

“This Congress alone, I’ve led more than a dozen bipartisan bills that put up immediate guardrails to keep pace with the rapid rise of AI,” Gottheimer said.

Gottheimer called on House leadership to bring Congress back before the election to consider AI safety legislation, including the measures he announced Friday.

Jay Edwards

Born and raised in Northwest NJ, Jay has a degree in Communications and has had a life-long interest in local radio and various styles of music. Jay has held numerous jobs over the years such as stunt car driver, bartender, voice-over artist, traffic reporter (award winning), NY Yankee maintenance crewmember and peanut farm worker. His hobbies include mountain climbing, snowmobiling, cooking, performing stand-up comedy and he is an avid squirrel watcher. Jay has been a guest on America’s Morning Headquarters,program on The Weather Channel, and was interviewed by Sam Champion.

sourceTexts.title: Government Relations Update — September 2026: Funding Forecast, AI Legislation, and the Midterm Elections
sourceTexts.text:
By

Samuel Burns - Internet2 Senior Policy Advisor

Estimated reading time: 9 minutes

This update covers the latest developments in the federal appropriations process, plans for bipartisan federal AI legislation, plus a preview of midterm elections and their potential impact on R&E.

The Status of Federal Science Funding in FY2027

Key Takeaways

Congress passed a continuing resolution (CR) which was signed into law on September 2, 2026.

This legislation funds the federal government through December 11 at FY2026 spending levels.

The CR contains a provision (Division A, Sec. 157) that prohibits the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) from implementing its planned revisions to federal grant-making rules that would have taken effect at the beginning of October.

The CR maintains the prohibition on changes to indirect cost rates that Congress adopted for FY2026 funding for National Science Foundation (NSF) and other agencies.

The CR gives effect to both provisions throughout its duration, but not past December 11, 2026.

Why This Matters to You

The IT leadership community: The CR delays implementation of new compliance standards for campuses that support federally funded research, giving IT leaders more time to prepare for and get clarity on the practical implications of new federal requirements.

The research & science community: The temporary block of OMB’s proposed grant-making revisions and the extension of protections for negotiated indirect cost rates provide months of additional stability to the federal research grant environment.

The public policy community: This legislation provides funding stability for critical R&E priorities.

The Deep Dive

Rather than engaging in the last-minute negotiations that have become increasingly common ahead of funding deadlines, both chambers of Congress elected to accept a CR weeks ahead of the end of the fiscal year. Leaders on Capitol Hill were eager to avoid the threat of a government shutdown in an election year; this swift resolution enabled many lawmakers to quickly shift focus to their re-election campaigns. The House has adjourned and will not be returning to Washington until after the midterms. The Senate is scheduled to remain in session through the end of September.

While Congress has provided funding stability through the next few months, many agencies still have billions of dollars of funding available that they are focused on obligating before the end of the fiscal year. Some agencies will also have carryover funding that will not expire on September 30, allowing them to continue advancing major initiatives going into the fall. Under the CR, agencies are allowed to continue to issue new funding solicitations and make awards with this funding, as long as it is not for new programs or activities.

Looking Ahead

The Senate has still not unveiled its proposed annual budget, and it is increasingly likely it will be delayed until after the midterms. The Senate is expected to reject the significant spending cuts called for in the Trump Administration’s FY2027 budget proposal from earlier this year, and will likely propose higher funding levels than those outlined in draft House legislation.

Meaningful progress on longer-term funding legislation is unlikely until after the midterms. It is likely that an additional CR will be necessary to extend funding beyond December 11, 2026.

Ultimately, the outcome of the elections will play a major role in determining the timing, structure, and overall direction of federal science funding for the remainder of FY2027 and beyond.

Signals from Capitol Hill on Federal AI Regulation

Key Takeaways

There is growing public pressure for federal legislators to take action on AI regulation and a growing sense among lawmakers that bipartisan legislation is necessary.

Congressman Jay Obernolte (R-CA-23) and Congresswoman Lori Trahan (D-MA-03) introduced the FRONTIER AI Act New Window IconDecorative icon to indicate a new browser window (opens in a new window) this summer, which has attracted attention among lawmakers in recent weeks.

The bill would create a third-party assessment process that would be embedded within frontier AI companies.

Congressman Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ-05) recently announced New Window IconDecorative icon to indicate a new browser window (opens in a new window) two new bipartisan AI safety bills, the American AI Security Act, with Rep. Mike Lawler (R-NY-17), and the China FIREWALL Act, with Rep. Nick LaLota (R-NY-01).

The American AI Security Act would create a mandatory 30-day government review process, led by the National Security Agency, for advanced AI models ahead of their release.

The China FIREWALL Act would ban the use of all Chinese-developed open-weight AI models on government-issued devices and would also prohibit federal agencies from procuring software that relies on those models.

Near-term action on these and other bills is unlikely, but this will be a major focus on Capitol Hill after the midterms.

Why This Matters to You

The IT leadership community: Congress is considering regulations that would provide new safeguards and guidance to enable IT leaders to better assess and utilize AI tools within their campus environments.

The research & science community: The federal government may adopt new measures that will impact what AI tools are available and how they are vetted for public use.

The public policy community: Congress is about to enter a period where it will need the expertise and perspective of the R&E community on the challenges and benefits of AI tools as it develops new regulatory frameworks.

The Deep Dive

Lawmakers are signaling that major action on AI will be a priority in the coming months. A wide range of proposals have already begun to circulate on Capitol Hill, with solutions ranging from voluntary guidelines to full hands-on reviews of models by federal agencies. While neither of the major political parties has articulated a clear vision for how the federal government should act to address public concerns about the potentially harmful impacts of frontier AI models, legislators are looking to work across party lines to ensure that swift action can be taken.

This provides a significant opportunity for members of the R&E community to share their advice, experience, and perspectives on how these tools are being utilized and what kind of support the community needs from the federal government to ensure a safe, secure, and productive AI-enabled working environment for researchers and educators. Members of Congress will be looking for input as they develop potential legislative solutions that may govern the development, adoption, and use of AI tools for years to come.

Much as they did following the proliferation of the internet, federal policymakers are approaching an inflection point at which new guidance, regulatory frameworks, and legislative action will be needed to address rapid technological change. Ensuring these policies reflect the needs of the R&E community will be a critical component of that effort.

Looking Ahead

Action on these priorities prior to the midterms is now off the table, as the House has adjourned weeks earlier than originally anticipated. Following the midterms, Congress will enter the so-called “lame duck” period where action on major new initiatives is unlikely. However, that time will be spent planning for the beginning of 2027 when newly elected legislators will be sworn in, and the new Congress will launch into a new cycle of high activity.

Midterm Election Forecast and What It Might Mean for R&E

Key Takeaways

The focus in Washington has now shifted toward re-election campaigns and which party will hold control of the two chambers of Congress starting in January 2027.

The House adjourned two weeks early, underscoring Speaker Mike Johnson’s view that additional time on the campaign trail will be critical for the most vulnerable members of his narrow majority.

The Senate will also adjourn soon to allow those running for re-election to return fully to the campaign trail.

Current forecasts and polling suggest the House is very likely to flip to Democratic control. It remains less likely, but still possible, that the Senate will also change hands.

The outcome of the midterm elections will have a number of practical implications for the R&E community and impact everything from funding levels to the implementation of requirements and guidance from federal grant-making and regulatory agencies.

Why This Matters to You

The IT leadership community: Efforts by the Administration to compel internal policy changes at universities and impose new requirements and standards on research activity may not hold under increased scrutiny from a new congressional majority.

The research & science community: Federal agency policy and funding changes impacting researchers and their work may be reversed, frozen, or subject to review if control in Congress changes.

The public policy community: Changes to the power dynamics on Capitol Hill will impact policy priorities and spending levels and will require new strategies to accomplish advocacy goals.

The Deep Dive

Change is likely coming to Washington as voter frustration with the Administration and current congressional majorities grows on issues ranging from immigration and foreign policy to economic conditions and cuts to federal programs. The balance of power in Congress currently sits at majorities of 219 Republicans to 214 Democrats in the House and 53 Republicans to 47 Democrats in the Senate. A shift of just three seats in the House and four seats in the Senate would mean a change in majority between parties. If Democrats do ultimately win control of either or both houses of Congress, the resulting divided government will have many implications for the R&E community.

A top priority will likely be increased oversight of federal agency activities in the form of investigations and public hearings. Committees driven by Democratic majorities and leadership will issue requests and subpoenas for documents, records, and testimony from agency leaders and White House officials to gather information and inform the public about many of the activities of the federal government over the last two years. In some cases, impeachments and removal of some officials from office may follow if evidence of significant wrongdoing is uncovered.

Stemming from these efforts, there will also be greater scrutiny of major Administration initiatives such as the Genesis Mission, agency staffing cuts initiated by DOGE, OMB’s proposed changes to grant-making rules, and the Department of Education’s efforts to force changes to university policies and priorities. Congressional committees will seek answers about how money has been spent, how decisions have been made, and what the impacts of various policies have been. This may lead to delays or changes to everything from rules and guidance to leadership at federal agencies as the White House responds to congressional pressure.

There will also be major implications for federal agency funding, particularly for agencies that support scientific research. With a divided government, White House budget plans will be even less likely to translate into final law without significant revisions or limitations as a result of negotiations with congressional leaders. Halts or reversals to many of the major cuts to research funding and changes to the agencies that manage those programs will likely follow.

Finally, bipartisanship will become a requirement to accomplish any major legislative solution. As Congress and the Administration contemplate the future of frontier AI models, investment in new tools and areas of research, and support for students and educators, they will need to collaborate and negotiate a viable path forward.

Looking Ahead

The midterm elections are only a few weeks away, but much can still happen to determine who controls each chamber of Congress and by what margin. Even a small shift in legislative seats could have a major impact on the fate and direction of ongoing and planned federal initiatives, funding levels, and tangible impacts for researchers, students, educators, and the community that supports them. October will be spent campaigning, but November and December will be spent planning for the flurry of activity that will come at the start of the new year.

Government Relations Updates are a recurring briefing from the Internet2 Government Relations team, breaking down federal policy developments, agency actions, and legislative advocacy to explain what’s happening in Washington and why it matters for the future of the research and higher education community.

Have questions? Contact us to connect with:

Belinda Nixon, Vice President and General Counsel

Matt Hall, Principal Policy Advisor & Analyst, for federal agency engagement, community policy initiatives, and Internet2’s broader federal engagement strategy

Sam Burns, Senior Policy Advisor, for congressional activity and the federal budget and appropriations process

Contact Us

About the Author(s)

Sam is a Senior Policy Advisor on Internet2’s Government Relations Team. He has nearly a decade of experience bridging the gap between federal policymakers and the R&E community by raising awareness, analyzing legislation, and helping to spotlight opportunities for collaboration. If you ever have a question about what’s going on in Washington, Sam’s your guy.
